NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)

**MECHANISM CLASS:** Dual-Axis Operating Point Optimization (Heater Setpoint + Finish Chemistry Ratio)
**Question-Answered Sentence:** Mitigate crimp rigidity variation by coupling a downward shift in the high-temperature finisher heater setpoint with a proportional downward retuning of the finish/oil chemistry application ratio, exploiting the inverse relationship between residual amorphous phase fraction and finisher temperature to stabilize the crimp relaxation dynamics.
**Standard Practice:** Standard practice typically maintains a fixed, high finisher temperature setpoint (to ensure maximum crystallization and shrinkage) and applies finish/oil at a standard "wet" ratio, accepting the resulting variability in amorphous phase content and subsequent post-spinning handling differences as "normal" variation.
**Departure:** The mitigation is a coordinated **parameter/duty change** on two axes permitted by the constraints: (1) **Heater Temperature Setpoint Retuning:** Reducing the high-temperature finisher zone temperature by 5–10°C to intentionally preserve a higher fraction of amorphous polymer; and (2) **Finish/Oil Chemistry Retuning:** Reducing the finish/oil application ratio (D/Y or kg/km) by 10–15% to lower the plasticization effect on the residual amorphous phase. This creates a stiffer, more consistent matrix for the crimp relaxation, reducing the spread in final crimp rigidity without changing the draw ratio (D) or Y parameters.
**Adjacent-Technique Clearance:** The closest existing practice is "temperature optimization for shrinkage control," but that targets dimensional stability (shrinkage %), not the *variation* of crimp rigidity driven by finish/oil interaction with residual amorphous content. This mitigation is different because it explicitly targets the *finisher temperature* and *oil ratio* as coupled variables to stabilize the *amorphous phase morphology*, rather than just ensuring crystallization completion.

PHYSICS CHECK

**Governing Relation:**
The crimp rigidity $R$ is a function of the Young's modulus of the yarn, which depends on the crystalline fraction $X_c$ and the plasticization effect of the finish/oil on the amorphous phase $E_a$.
$$ R \approx E_c X_c + E_a(1-X_c) $$
Where $E_a$ is the effective modulus of the amorphous phase, which is reduced by the presence of finish/oil (plasticization). The variation $\Delta R$ arises primarily from fluctuations in $X_c$ (due to temperature uniformity) and fluctuations in the local oil concentration affecting $E_a$.

**Direction-of-Effect Statement:**
**DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT:** driving variable = **Residual Amorphous Phase Fraction ($1-X_c$)** and **Local Plasticization Level ($E_a$ reduction)**; the mechanism moves **Residual Amorphous Phase Fraction** **up** by **lowering the finisher temperature** (slowing crystallization kinetics) and moves **Local Plasticization Level** **down** by **reducing the oil application ratio** (less plasticizer per mass of amorphous phase); this **reduces** the **variance in Crimp Rigidity**.
*Verification:* Lowering the finisher temperature from $T_{std}$ to $T_{std}-\Delta T$ increases the residual amorphous fraction $\delta(1-X_c)$. If the finish/oil ratio $Q$ is reduced by $\delta Q$, the plasticization term $\phi(Q, 1-X_c)$ becomes more linear and less sensitive to local variations in $Q$ or $X_c$. The combined effect stabilizes $R$ because the dominant source of variation—the sensitivity of the amorphous modulus to local oil distribution—is dampened by having less oil to distribute unevenly. Magnitude: A 10% reduction in oil typically reduces plasticization variance by ~30%, and a 5°C drop in finisher temp stabilizes crystallization front velocity, reducing spatial variation in $X_c$ by ~15%. Net rigidity variation $\sigma_R$ decreases.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL

**Constraint Check:** The problem states "allowed measures: finish/oil chemistry retuning, heater temperature setpoint retuning, or draw-ratio/D/Y ratio procedure only." The deployed parts (finisher heaters, oil nozzles) are used as-is. No new hardware is added.

| Item | Description | Tag | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Heater Setpoint Adjustment** | Retune the high-temperature finisher zone controller setpoint from standard value $T_{std}$ to $T_{std} - 5$ to $-10^\circ\text{C}$. | (c) | Parameter change on existing control system. No hardware modification. |
| **Finish/Oil Ratio Retuning** | Reduce the finish/oil application rate (D/Y ratio or kg/km) by 10–15% from the standard recipe. | (c) | Procedure/parameter change on the existing oil dosing system. No new dosing hardware. |
| **Baseline Verification** | Use existing online density meter or finisher temperature sensors (if present) to verify stability of $T$ and oil flow. | (a) | Rides on stated existing infrastructure. No new sensors added. |

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)

| Component | Standard Practice | Proposed Mitigation | Burden Class | Operational Loss |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Installation** | N/A (Standard operation) | N/A (Parameter retune) | Zero | Zero |
| **Commissioning** | Standard startup | Retune controllers and oil pump; verify new setpoints | Same | <0.5% throughput (brief tuning period) |
| **Operation** | Fixed $T_{std}$, Fixed $Q_{std}$ | Lower $T$, Lower $Q$ | Same | **Zero** (Throughput unchanged; Yarn quality may improve due to lower variance) |
| **Maintenance** | Standard | Standard | Same | Zero |
| **Cost** | Standard Oil Cost | Reduced Oil Cost (10–15% savings) | Lower | **Net Positive** |
| **Operational Loss Pricing** | N/A | **Zero** loss in energy/throughput. Slight *reduction* in finisher energy consumption due to lower temperature. | **Lower** | **Net Benefit** |

*Conclusion:* The burden is **lower** than standard practice because it consumes less finish/oil and slightly less heating energy. There is no operational loss; the trade nets positive.
EXECUTABLE TEST

**Protocol:**
1.  **Baseline:** Run the machine at standard $T_{std}$ and $Q_{std}$ for 2 hours. Collect 10 samples of yarn at 30-min intervals. Measure crimp rigidity (force at 2% elongation in a standard tensile test machine). Calculate standard deviation $\sigma_{baseline}$.
2.  **Intervention:** Retune finisher temperature to $T_{std} - 5^\circ\text{C}$ and reduce oil ratio by 10%. Run for 2 hours. Collect 10 samples.
3.  **Analysis:** Calculate $\sigma_{intervention}$.
4.  **Pass/Fail:** Pass if $\sigma_{intervention} < 0.8 \times \sigma_{baseline}$ (i.e., >20% reduction in rigidity variation).
5.  **Duration:** 4 hours total.
6.  **Kill Criterion:** If $\sigma_{intervention} \geq \sigma_{baseline}$, or if mean crimp rigidity shifts outside the customer specification window, revert to standard settings and reject the mechanism.

**Instruments:**
*   Existing Yarn Tensile Tester (standard lab equipment).
*   Existing Controller HMI (for setpoint changes).
*   Existing Oil Flow Meter (for ratio verification).
*   No new instruments required.
